2310.text: H8426 co-occurs with M41 (proclaim/hear) and M48 (wondrous deeds). First pass: thanksgiving here is the content proclaimed aloud (M41 supplies the act of proclaiming), directed at recounting the wondrous deeds (M48) -- H8426 names the substance of what is proclaimed and told.

2549.text: In Ps 30:12, other M-codes present are M22 (glory, singing praise) and M33/M55 (silence/stillness, negated); thanksgiving stands as the positive resolve set against silence, complementing glory's singing but functioning as the verbal counterpart distinct from song imagery.

2972.text: Across its full occurrence list H8426 clusters into three recurring realizations of one lexeme: (1) the concrete thank-offering sacrifice (Lev.7.12 x2, Lev.7.13, Lev.7.15, Lev.22.29, Ps.50.14, Ps.50.23, Ps.107.22, Ps.116.17, Amos.4.5, Jonah.2.9, 2Chr.29.31 x2, 2Chr.33.16, Jer.17.26, Jer.33.11), (2) the vocal/manner accompaniment of praise, 'with/in thanksgiving' (Ps.69.30, Ps.26.7, Ps.95.2, Ps.100.4, Ps.147.7, Isa.51.3), and (3) the institutional thanksgiving choir/procession/company (Neh.12.27, Neh.12.31, Neh.12.38, Neh.12.40, Ps.42.4). A fourth, rarer sense realizes it as verbal confession (Josh.7.19, Ezra.10.11). This is a single strong showing internally the full sense-range attributed to the subgroup label (hymn, choir, offering) without needing a second member strong to supply any of these senses.

2973.text: Since H8426 is the sole member strong of this subgroup, there is no second lexeme to compare it against directly; the meaningful cross-comparison available is internal -- between H8426's own sacrificial/cultic-object occurrences (e.g. Lev.7.12-15, Lev.22.29, 2Chr.29.31, 2Chr.33.16, Jer.17.26, Jer.33.11, Amos.4.5) versus its choir/procession-as-institution occurrences (Neh.12.27-40, Ps.42.4) versus its purely adverbial/manner occurrences ('with thanksgiving', e.g. Ps.69.30, Ps.95.2, Ps.100.4, Ps.147.7, Ps.26.7). These three groupings do not overlap grammatically: the sacrificial sense is always the head noun or a construct-genitive qualifier of an offering-word (zebach, shelamim), the choir sense functions as a collective-body noun (subject or object of appointment/movement verbs), and the manner sense is marked by a preposition (b-) modifying a separate main verb of praise. No morphological distinction (all occurrences are the same feminine noun stem, singular or plural absolute/construct) drives this three-way split -- it is purely syntactic/contextual, meaning the noun's referent is disambiguated entirely by its syntactic role in each verse rather than by any inflectional change.

3152.text: Yes -- todah operates through speech in several occurrences: Joshua commands Achan to 'give praise' (todah) and confess (Josh.7.19); Ezra's Nehemiah-parallel calls the people to 'make confession' (Ezra.10.11); and Ps.26.7 speaks of 'proclaiming thanksgiving aloud.' The characteristic is thus frequently commanded or addressed as a speech-act, not only performed ritually.

3165.text: Todah engages the vocal/speech level (song, proclamation, confession -- Ps.26.7, Ps.147.7, Josh.7.19) and the bodily/ritual-action level (sacrifice offered, loaves brought -- Lev.7.12-15) but the evidence never depicts it engaging a purely internal/unspoken level in isolation -- it is always externalized, either in speech or material offering, showing its seat is fundamentally expressive rather than private. Where a body link exists (the sacrificial act), it is functional -- the body/materials serve as the vehicle carrying the inner acknowledgment into concrete cultic form.

3177.text: Todah consistently engages the faculties of speech/voice (song, proclamation, confession) and volition (willing heart, vows performed) but never engages the intellect in an abstract or reasoning sense -- it is not depicted as a conclusion of argument but as a response of will and voice to perceived divine benefit or exposed guilt, showing the characteristic's nature as fundamentally responsive and expressive rather than deliberative.

12514.text: The looking-ahead words are used most often against another person. It is placed in the heart: "let none of you devise evil against another in your heart" (Zec 7:10), "do not devise evil in your hearts against one another" (Zec 8:17). It is done together: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (Jer 18:18); "In Heshbon they planned disaster against her" (Jer 48:2); "they made plans to put him to death" (Joh 11:53), and Lazarus as well (Joh 12:10); "The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners" (Act 27:42). It is aimed at the righteous and the weak: "The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him" (Psa 37:12); "who have planned to trip up my feet" (Psa 140:4). It hides behind a friendly word: "Come and let us meet together" "But they intended to do me harm" (Neh 6:2); Saul's bride-price, "Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines" (1Sa 18:25). It is pinned on the other side: "you and the Jews intend to rebel" (Neh 6:6). Another pleads against it: Esther "pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman" (Est 8:3; 9:24).

14181.text: Part 2 verses: what they add: Kin offence hardens. "A brother offended is more unyielding than a strong city, and quarreling is like the bars of a castle" (Pro 18:19). The closer the tie, the harder the wall. This is the reverse of Gen 13's reason for yielding ("for we are kinsmen"); Brothers' anger takes the form of imposed labour: "My mother's sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept!" (Song 1:6). The anger is felt by the one it lands on as the loss of her own vineyard. The next verse turns straight to "you whom my soul loves" (1:7); Edom against his brother: anger that never turns away. Edom "pursued his brother with the sword and cast off all pity, and his anger tore perpetually, and he kept his wrath forever" (Amo 1:11). God will deal with Edom "according to the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred against them" (Eze 35:11), with its speech: "They are given us to devour" (35:12); This is exactly the opposite of Gen 27:44–45. There Rebekah waits for Esau's anger to "turn away" and for him to "forget", and it does (Gen 33:4). Esau the man let his anger pass. Edom, his nation, "kept his wrath forever". The same bloodline shows anger's two courses; Amo 1:9 names the same failure for Tyre: "did not remember the covenant of brotherhood"; Anger at a brother judged like murder, and the remedy is reconciliation before worship: "everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment" (Mat 5:22); "leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother" (5:24). The worship waits on the relationship; Brothers in the work part without the yielding: "there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark … but Paul chose Silas" (Act 15:39–40). It began over Mark, "who had withdrawn from them" (15:38). Separation, as in Gen 13:11, but here neither party gives the other the choice. Both are "commended … to the grace of the Lord" (15:40) and the work goes on in two directions; Seat : none in-verse or ±2. The next verse after Song 1:6 has "you whom my soul loves" (Song 1:7). Genuine. The bearer's own. The one who bears her brothers' anger turns at once to the one her soul loves.

Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you" (Pro 9:7–8). The same rebuke brings out hate in one and love in the other; Wisdom in vain. "A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding" (Pro 14:6). He seeks, and does not find; Learning by his fall; "Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence" (19:25); "When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise" (21:11); The scoffer is not the one who learns. Others learn from what happens to him; Strife. "Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease" (Pro 22:10). "the scoffer is an abomination to mankind" (24:9); Justice and the guilt offering; "A worthless witness mocks at justice" (19:28). "Condemnation is ready for scoffers" (19:29); "Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance" (14:9). They mock the very means of putting guilt right; Delight, and the offer. "How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing ... If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you" (Pro 1:22–23). Scoffing is a delight held on to, and the offer still stands to the one who turns; Alone. "If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it" (Pro 9:12); The seat. As with Eliab in batch 2, the verses do not settle that it is true of Job; "Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor" (Pro 3:34, carried). This is the source of Jam 4:6 and 1Pe 5:5.

15213.text: The mocker mocked. Of Sennacherib, who mocked the Lord: "She despises you, she scorns you — the virgin daughter of Zion; she wags her head behind you" (2Ki 19:21; Isa 37:22). Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal: "Cry aloud, for he is a god ... perhaps he is asleep", and "there was no voice. No one answered" (1Ki 18:27, 29): I read: mocking here exposes a false claim, of a king who rose against the Holy One, and of a god who does not answer.

15237.text: A pride word is used of God here. lāʿag "mock" and lîṣ "scorn" are said of God: "the Lord holds them in derision" (Psa 2:4); "you hold all the nations in derision" (Psa 59:8); "Toward the scorners he is scornful" (Pro 3:34); wisdom: "I will mock when terror strikes you" (Pro 1:26); The verses show how God's derision differs from human mocking; Where it comes from. It comes from the one who "sits in the heavens" (Psa 2:4), from the height that batches 1–3 found is his by nature; What it answers. It always answers a rising against him: kings set "against the Lord and against his Anointed" (Psa 2:2), those of whom it says "'Who,' they think, 'will hear us?'" (Psa 59:7), the scorners (Pro 3:34), those who "refused to listen" (Pro 1:24); Whom it never targets. In these verses it is never aimed at the weak, the poor or the sufferer. Human mocking is aimed at exactly those: the poor (Pro 17:5), a father (Pro 30:17), the sufferer (Psa 22:7), builders called "feeble" (Neh 4:2); I read: God's derision is the laughter of the undisputed height at a dispute that cannot succeed. Human mockery is a self-made height looking down on someone made low; God is not mocked. "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked" (Gal 6:7). The mocking of his messengers goes on "until there was no remedy" (2Ch 36:16). This is the batch 1 point again: God's standing is challenged, and is not overturned; The Son is mocked, and does not answer in kind; The one with the undisputed standing is mocked on that very standing: "Hail, King of the Jews!" (Mat 27:29); "He saved others; he cannot save himself" (Mar 15:31); He "made no answer" (Luk 23:9), and he prays "Father, forgive them" (Luk 23:34); I read: in the Son, the majesty of batch 1 does not defend itself against mockery. This is the clearest instance of 13.1 Lowering himself in these words. It joins the batch 1 point that his majesty and his being "delivered into the hands of men" stand side by side (Luk 9:43–44); Mocking exposes a false height. Zion scorns Sennacherib (2Ki 19:21). Elijah mocks a god who does not answer (1Ki 18:27). Here the mocking does not come from pride. It names a claim that is empty.

16988.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch F [Claude reading]: Relating to others is most often a matter of the soul.; Souls are knit (1Sa 18:1).; A soul loves, seeks and fails (Song 3; 5).; Malice lives in the soul (Eze 25:6, 15).; Souls abhor each other, even God's soul and the people's (Lev 26).; One loves another "as one's own soul".; The heart is where hatred starts and is spoken (Lev 19:17; Gen 27:41). It is also where the response to another's fall is judged (Pro 24:17).; The human spirit registers bonds and bearing.; It is unsettled by a friend's absence and refreshed by a friend's arrival (2Co 2:13; 7:13; 1Co 16:18).; It is the manner of approach — gentleness (1Co 4:21).; It is what the wise hold back and the fool vents (Pro 29:11).; Sequences matter more than single verses. Reading before and after changed the picture in six places: 1Sa 18 (Jonathan and Saul); Lev 26 (reciprocal abhorrence broken by God); Psa 143 and Psa 51 (the crushing chains); Judg 19 and the other merry-heart narratives (threshold states); 2Co 2 → 7 (the spirit's rest through persons); 2Ki 2 (spirit transfer confirmed by others); Meaning shifts with circumstance in consistent ways: *crush*: by whom, and turned to whom (§5); *tender heart*: to what it yields (§6); *good heart*: from God or from wine (§7); *love / hate one's soul*: well-being vs clinging (§3); *hāgâ*: what the heart rehearses (§12.2); *nûaḥ*: what rests in or on the person (§9.5); Inner states spread between people: the fainthearted soldier melts others (Deu 20:8); heart-speech is reported (Gen 27:42); a lowly heart gives rest to other souls (Mat 11:29); a congregation refreshes Titus's spirit (2Co 7:13); the prophet's heart takes in the people's doom (Jer 4:18–19); Other spirits relate to people as occupants of a house (Mat 12:43–45) and as seizures between people (1Sa 18:10; Judg 9:23 in Batch D). The divine Spirit rests upon people and is recognised by others (Num 11; 2Ki 2).; Fringe worth keeping: the knit soul beside the seizing spirit in one chapter (1Sa 18); the heart awake while the body lags (Song 5); God refusing to complete reciprocal abhorrence (Lev 26:44); Jezebel curing a vexed spirit by a manufactured good heart (1Ki 21); the prophet's heart for Moab set against Ammon's malice of soul (Isa 15; Jer 48; Eze 25); past hatred as a legal criterion (Deu 19)

What the soul characteristically does: *Needs and seeks:* thirsts, longs, pants, faints (Psa 107:5; 119:81; Isa 26:8–9), waits (Psa 33:20; 62:1, 5; 130:5–6), hopes (Lam 3:24), clings (Psa 63:8; 119:25 "clings to the dust").; *Suffers:*; bitter (1Sa 1:10; 22:2; 30:6; Job 3:20; 7:11; 10:1; 21:25; 27:2; Isa 38:15; Eze 27:31); cast down, in turmoil (Psa 42:5, 6, 11; 43:5); bowed down (Psa 44:25; 57:6; Lam 3:20); poured out (1Sa 1:15; Job 30:16; Psa 42:4; Isa 53:12 "poured out his soul to death"); refuses comfort (Psa 77:2); is troubled (Psa 6:3; Joh 12:27); "very sorrowful, even to death" (Mat 26:38; Mar 14:34); "my soul is bereft of peace; I have forgotten what happiness is" (Lam 3:17); "vexed to death" (Judg 16:16); *Responds with joy and worship:* rejoices and exults (Isa 61:10; Psa 35:9); boasts in the Lord (Psa 34:2); blesses the Lord (Psa 103:1–2, 22; 104:1, 35; 146:1); "My soul magnifies the Lord" (Luk 1:46); keeps testimonies (Psa 119:129, 167); knows (Psa 139:14).; *Loves and hates:* "the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David" (1Sa 18:1); "his soul hates the wicked" (Psa 11:5); "soul abhors" (Lev 26:15, 43); "malice of soul" (Eze 25:6, 15).; *Is satisfied or not:* Psa 63:5; 107:9; Jer 31:14, 25; Ecc 6:3; Pro 13:4.; *Is lifted up:* "To you, O Lord, I lift up my soul" (Psa 25:1; 86:4; 143:8); contrast "who does not lift up his soul to what is false" (Psa 24:4).; *Is addressed by its owner* — fringe, but many verses: "Why are you cast down, O my soul?" (Psa 42:5, 11; 43:5); "Bless the Lord, O my soul" (Psa 103:1); "Return, O my soul, to your rest" (Psa 116:7); "For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence" (Psa 62:5); "I have calmed and quieted my soul" (Psa 131:2); "March on, my soul, with might!" (Judg 5:21); The rich fool: "I will say to my soul, 'Soul, … relax, eat, drink, be merry'" (Luk 12:19); [Claude reading] The soul is something a person can stand beside, speak to, quiet and command. There is an "I" that addresses "my soul".

17258.text: d. Soul and death: "as her soul was departing (for she was dying)" (Gen 35:18); "you will not abandon my soul to Sheol" (Psa 16:10; Act 2:27); "brought up my soul from Sheol" (Psa 30:3); soul // life near the pit (Job 33:18, 22, 28, 30); "my soul would soon have lived in the land of silence" (Psa 94:17); "This night your soul is required of you" (Luk 12:20); "forfeit his soul" (Mat 16:26; Mar 8:36–37); "do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Mat 10:28); "the souls of those who had been slain" under the altar (Rev 6:9; 20:4)

17264.text: e. Wind and breath in relation to the inner being — explicitly retained per the researcher: *Breath = life in flesh:*; "all flesh in which is the breath of life" (Gen 6:17; 7:15, 22); "sinews … flesh … skin … But there was no breath in them" → "breath came into them, and they lived" (Eze 37:6–10); "When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust" (Psa 104:29); *Breath and thought:* "When his breath departs, he returns to the earth; on that very day his plans perish" (Psa 146:4). Link to the thought vocabulary (see brief §5).; *Breath as frailty:* "Remember that my life is a breath" (Job 7:7); "They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts" (Ecc 3:19); "He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again" (Psa 78:39).; *No breath = no inner life:* idols have "no breath in them" (Jer 10:14; 51:17; Hab 2:19; Psa 135:17). fringe: "there was no more breath in her" = the queen of Sheba overwhelmed (1Ki 10:5; 2Ch 9:4).; *Wind as the emptiness of inner striving* (Ecclesiastes): "I applied my heart to know wisdom … this also is but a striving after wind" (Ecc 1:17); the same in 1:14; 2:11, 17, 26; 4:4, 6, 16; 5:16; "Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind" (Ecc 6:9) — appetite (nephesh) + wind; *Wind as empty words:*; "windy knowledge … fill his belly with the east wind" (Job 15:2); "windy words" (Job 16:3); "the speech of a despairing man is wind" (Job 6:26); "the words of your mouth be a great wind" (Job 8:2); "The prophets will become wind; the word is not in them" (Jer 5:13); "utter wind and lies" (Mic 2:11); *Wind as empty outcome:* "we have given birth to wind" (Isa 26:18); "Whoever troubles his own household will inherit the wind" (Pro 11:29); "sow the wind, and … reap the whirlwind" (Hos 8:7); "Ephraim feeds on the wind" (Hos 12:1).; *Wind as the image for a shaken heart:* "the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind" (Isa 7:2).; *Wind and lust:* "a wild donkey … in her heat sniffing the wind! Who can restrain her lust?" (Jer 2:24); "to restrain her is to restrain the wind" (Pro 27:16).

17274.text: 3.4 Distinction — where the text separates the components: *Division of soul and spirit (Heb 4:12):* "piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart." [Claude reading] Soul and spirit are close enough that only the word of God can separate them, just as joints and marrow are adjacent parts of the body. The heart is where the *thoughts and intentions* are, and they are *discerned* there.; *Living soul vs life-giving spirit:* "The first man Adam became a living being [psychē]; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit" (1Co 15:45; cf. Gen 2:7).; *Spirit vs mind:* 1Co 14:14–15 (above).; *Spirit vs flesh (as kind):*; "a spirit does not have flesh and bones" (Luk 24:39); "horses are flesh, and not spirit" (Isa 31:3); "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit" (Joh 3:6); "the flesh is no help at all" (Joh 6:63); "put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit" (1Pe 3:18; 4:6); "the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved" (1Co 5:5); *Soul vs body:* "cannot kill the soul" (Mat 10:28).; *Spirit vs body in place:* "absent in body, … present in spirit" (1Co 5:3–4; Col 2:5). fringe [Claude reading]: the spirit can be "with" people where the body is not.; *Inner vs outer:*; "Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day" (2Co 4:16, with "lose heart"); "a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit" (Rom 2:29); "the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (1Pe 3:4); "man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart" (1Sa 16:7); "what is in the heart" vs "outward appearance" (2Co 5:12); *Food and the heart:* "since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled" (Mar 7:19). The text draws a boundary: food goes to the stomach, not the heart. But see §3.6, where food *does* strengthen the heart.

17278.text: 3.7 Containment — what is placed "in" what: *In the heart:*; law, words, commandments (Deu 6:6; Psa 37:31; 119:11; Jer 31:33); wisdom (Pro 2:10; 14:33); fear of God (Jer 32:40); eternity (Ecc 3:11); idols (Eze 14:3); deceit (Pro 12:20); folly (Pro 22:15); anger (Ecc 7:9); the Spirit (2Co 1:22; Gal 4:6); Christ "may dwell in your hearts through faith" (Eph 3:17); "the peace of Christ rule in your hearts" (Col 3:15); "the word of Christ dwell in you richly … thankfulness in your hearts" (Col 3:16); God's love "poured into our hearts" (Rom 5:5); what "the devil had already put into the heart of Judas" (Joh 13:2); what "God has put into their hearts" (Rev 17:17; Neh 2:12; 7:5; Ezr 7:27; 2Co 8:16); *Within me:* spirit (Psa 143:4; Isa 26:9; Job 32:18; Dan 7:15); soul (Psa 42:5–6; 131:2); heart (Psa 22:14; 39:3; 109:22; Jer 8:18; 23:9; Lam 1:20; Hos 11:8).; *Spirit and heart inside flesh:* "I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh" (Eze 36:26); "put breath in you" (Eze 37:6).; *Spirit and body:* "your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you" (1Co 6:19); "if the Spirit … dwells in you, he … will also give life to your mortal bodies" (Rom 8:11).; [Claude reading] The heart is the innermost *location* in the text's picture. Soul-states, spirit, God's Spirit, words, law and dispositions are placed "in" it. Spirit and soul are also spoken of as "within me", but they are less often described as containers.

17282.text: 4. Fringe observations collected (quick list): Heart = "midst" of sea, heaven, earth; the inner seat named as the *middle* (§2.1a).; Aaron carries the tribes "on his heart" before the Lord (Exo 28:29–30).; "I slept, but my heart was awake" (Song 5:2).; "Eyes of your hearts" (Eph 1:18); morning star rising in hearts (2Pe 1:19); a veil over hearts (2Co 3:15).; "Walls of my heart" (Jer 4:19); "tear open their breast" (Hos 13:8); a man without self-control = "a city … without walls" (Pro 25:28, rûaḥ). The inner seat is imaged as an enclosure.; Nabal's heart "died within him, and he became as a stone" after the wine left (1Sa 25:37).; Nephesh = neck/throat (Psa 69:1; 105:18) and = corpse (Num 19:11).; Knife to the throat "if you are given to appetite" (Pro 23:2).; Sheol's "appetite" and "mouth" (Isa 5:14).; "Perfume boxes" tagged nephesh (Isa 3:20).; A millstone in pledge = "a life in pledge" (Deu 24:6).; The soul addressed by its owner (Psa 42; 103; 116:7; 131:2; Luk 12:19).; rûaḥ = compass *side* (1Ch 9:24; Eze 42:16–20).; rûaḥ = "cool" of the day when God walked in the garden (Gen 3:8).; Dispositions as "spirits" that come upon a person: jealousy, whoredom, confusion, deep sleep, stupor, skill, grace (§2.3c).; Spirits causing muteness or a bent back (Mar 9:17; Luk 13:11).; "A spirit glided past my face; the hair of my flesh stood up" (Job 4:15).; "Present in spirit" though absent in body (1Co 5:3; Col 2:5).; Spirit of Elijah on Elisha; Moses' Spirit shared with the elders (2Ki 2; Num 11).; Queen of Sheba: "there was no more breath in her" (1Ki 10:5).; Man's heart/mind exchanged for a beast's (Dan 4:16; 5:21; 7:4).; "The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy" (Pro 14:10) — the privacy of the inner seat.; "As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man" (Pro 27:19).; "He has put eternity into man's heart" (Ecc 3:11).; Spirit-birth pictured by the wind (Joh 3:8).; Plans perish when the breath departs (Psa 146:4) — breath and thought.; Bread strengthens the heart (Judg 19:5; Psa 104:15), yet food "enters not his heart but his stomach" (Mar 7:19), and the heart should be strengthened "by grace, not by foods" (Heb 13:9). Three verses, three angles on the same relation.; The bosom holds both loved ones and anger or insults (Ecc 7:9; Psa 89:50).; "Conscience" also = "consciousness / mindful" (Heb 10:2; 1Pe 2:19).

19213.text: How it co-exists.; Petition is the most common companion: "Hide not your face from me" (Psa 27:9; 69:17 "for I am in distress"; 102:2 "in the day of my distress"; 143:7).; Petition reversed: "Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities" (Psa 51:9), then "Create in me a clean heart" (51:10). The penitent asks God to hide his face from the sin, not from the self: the same act, wished in the opposite direction.; A false inference: the wicked "says in his heart, 'God has forgotten, he has hidden his face, he will never see it'" (Psa 10:11). He reads hiddenness as licence.; Its denial as resolution: "he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard, when he cried to him" (Psa 22:24).; Waiting and hope through it: "I will wait for the Lord, who is hiding his face … and I will hope in him" (Isa 8:17). "Truly, you are a God who hides himself, O God of Israel, the Savior" (Isa 45:15) holds hiddenness and saving together. Job 34:29 (Elihu): "When he hides his face, who can behold him".

19224.text: (a) Concealing one's own wrong. Each case has its own sequence: Achan: "when I saw … then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent" (Jos 7:21); Joshua: "tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me" (7:19); Achan: "Truly I have sinned" (7:20); "behold, it was hidden in his tent" (7:22); Seeing, coveting, taking, hiding, being demanded to disclose, confessing, being found.; Moses: "He looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand" (Exo 2:12). When the deed surfaces: "Moses was afraid, and thought, 'Surely the thing is known'" (2:14). Concealment fails, and fear follows.; The hidden adultery: "it is hidden from the eyes of her husband" (Num 5:13). The next verse: "the spirit of jealousy comes over him" (5:14). Where a deed is hidden, suspicion grows in the other person.; Job's denial: "if I have concealed my transgressions as others do by hiding my iniquity in my heart [*chob*, bosom], because I stood in great fear of the multitude, and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silence" (Job 31:33–34). The verse names the motive for concealing sin: fear of social contempt. Job denies he acted on it.; The lepers: they hid the plunder (2Ki 7:8), then "said to one another, 'We are not doing right … If we are silent … punishment will overtake us'" (7:9). Conscience reverses concealment into telling.; Concealment as savouring: "Though evil is sweet in his mouth, though he hides it under his tongue, though he is loath to let it go and holds it in his mouth" (Job 20:12–13). The hidden sin is kept because it is enjoyed.; Not hiding at all: "the look on their faces bears witness against them; they proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it" (Isa 3:9). The face discloses: shamelessness.

19230.text: How it co-exists. Fear is the most frequent companion, on both sides: fear drives concealment (Job 31:34; Mat 25:25), or follows its failure (Exo 2:14); fear blocks disclosure until it is overcome (1Sa 3:15–18); Joy (Mat 13:44), enjoyment of sin (Job 20:12–13) and conscience (2Ki 7:9) are the other companions.

19252.text: (g) Dread of an anticipated harm (*da'ag*, *de'agah*).; The Transjordan tribes built an altar "from fear that in time to come your children might say to our children, 'What have you to do with the Lord'" (Jos 22:24), "so your children might make our children cease to worship the Lord" (22:25). Anxiety about a future break in worship leads to a preventive act.; "I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted … lest I be handed over to them" (Jer 38:19). Jeremiah answers: "Obey now the voice of the Lord" (38:20). Dread of people stands against obedience.; "the famine of which you are afraid shall follow close after you to Egypt" (Jer 42:16), from those who said "we will go to the land of Egypt, where we shall not … be hungry" (42:14). Fleeing the feared thing brings it along.; "Whom did you dread and fear, so that you lied, and did not remember me, did not lay it to heart?" (Isa 57:11). Dread leads to lying, and lying to forgetting God.; "they melt in fear, they are troubled like the sea that cannot be quiet" (Jer 49:23), after hearing bad news.; The same word turned to sin: "I confess my iniquity; I am sorry [*da'ag*] for my sin" (Psa 38:18). Anxiety becomes contrition.

19256.text: Strand (b), a divine Spirit replaces the anxious speaker's own seat. Mat 10:19 → 10:20 "it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you". Batch E v2 §1.6 ("The Spirit speaks through the person"). The anxiety about what to say is answered by another's Spirit in the speaker's place. The Luke parallel runs the same way: Luk 12:11 → 12:12 "for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say". Luke gives the answer as teaching: the Spirit supplies the knowing that the anxiety lacked.; Strand (e), the choked hearer is set between two hearts — new in v3. Luk 8:14 (the thorns) stands between "the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts" (8:12) and "hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience" (8:15). The cares act on a heart where the word has been sown, and the contrast the passage draws is with a good heart that holds the word fast. Mat 13:22 ← 13:19 "snatches away what has been sown in his heart" is the same frame (v1 §2 *merimna* row).; The man who is not anxious. Jer 17:8 is framed by "whose heart turns away from the Lord" (17:5), and by "The heart is deceitful … I the Lord search the heart and test the mind" (17:9–10) (v1 §2 *de'agah* row). The unanxious tree stands between two statements about the heart.; Strand (g), a neighbouring oracle's heart. Jer 49:23 (Hamath and Arpad "melt in fear, they are troubled like the sea") follows 49:22, the end of the oracle against Edom: "the heart of the warriors of Edom shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains". The party is different: Edom in 49:22, the cities of Damascus in 49:23. So the seat does not belong to the anxious ones of 49:23. What the two oracles share is the same collapse under bad news. It is stated as a heart in labour for Edom's warriors, and as melting and a troubled sea for Hamath. It is recorded as a parallel, not as the seat of 49:23.; Spurious context link: Jer 38:19 → 38:17 "your life shall be spared". *Nephesh* is bodily life here: the life Zedekiah fears to lose. It names what the dread is about, not a seat.

19299.text: 2Ki 7:8–9: taking and hiding plunder → "we are not doing right" → telling

19354.text: Jer 49:23 (AX) | Jer 49:22 "heart of the warriors of Edom" | a different party (Edom) · genuine | §11 Seat (parallel only)

19505.text: Remember. *"Remember the wondrous works that he has done … children of Jacob, his chosen ones!"* (Psa 105:5–6); *"Remember these things, O Jacob … you will not be forgotten by me"* (Isa 44:21). Another person can take on the reminding: *"I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things"* (2Pe 1:15).

19606.text: Psalm 105:43: "his chosen ones with singing": Psalm 105 is a call to remember. It is addressed to the chosen: *"Remember the wondrous works that he has done … O offspring of Abraham, his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!"* (v5–6). It starts with the heart: *"let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice!"* (v3).; The psalm's reason is God's own remembering: *"He remembers his covenant forever"* (v8); *"For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant"* (v42); The verse follows straight on: *"So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing"* (v43). The joy and singing are set on the people brought out. They come with being brought out, and the bringing out comes from God remembering his promise. The chosen are told to remember (v5) because he remembered (v8, v42).; On the way there the psalm tells one man's inward testing: *"His feet were hurt with fetters … until what he had said came to pass, the word of the Lord tested him"* (v18–19). That man was Joseph, sent ahead of the chosen.; Psalm 105 tells nothing of the people's failures. It has *"none among his tribes who stumbled"* (v37). Its last verse states the purpose of the whole: *"that they might keep his statutes and observe his laws"* (v45).

19614.text: The return is the Lord's remembering. He remembered his covenant at their cry (Psa 106:44–45). He remembered his promise and brought them out with joy (Psa 105:42–43). He blots out their sins and will not remember them (Isa 43:25). The chosen are called to remember in turn (Psa 105:5; Isa 44:21).

19636.text: Isaiah 45:4: "I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me": The oracle is to Cyrus: *"Thus says the Lord to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped"* (v1). The choosing is of Israel: *"For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me"* (v4). "Chosen" is *bāḥîr* (H0972).; Cyrus is the other, called for the sake of the chosen. Twice he is told he does not know God: *"I name you, though you do not know me"* (v4); *"I equip you, though you do not know me"* (v5); Knowing is the purpose twice: for Cyrus: *"that you may know that it is I, the Lord, the God of Israel, who call you by your name"* (v3); for all peoples: *"that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me"* (v6)

19651.text: Isaiah 7:15–16 — "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good": The setting is a king’s heart in fear. Syria and Ephraim are marching on Jerusalem, and *"the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind"* (v2). The Lord sends Isaiah with a word for that heart: *"Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint"* (v4); the threat *"shall not stand"* (v7); then the condition: *"If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all"* (v9). Both "firm" words are the one verb (H0539), so standing firm and being kept firm are the same word.; Then the Lord makes Ahaz an offer: *"Ask a sign of the Lord your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven"* (v11). Ahaz refuses, in pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (v12). The answer shows what that refusal was: *"Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?"* (v13). Ahaz’s refusal was a choice. He chose not to take hold of what the Lord held out.; The sign is given anyway, and at its centre is a child who has what Ahaz lacked: *"He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (v15). The act is one act with two sides: refusing the evil (H3988A); choosing the good (H0977); Refusing is not a step before the choice. It is the choice seen from the other side. Both rest on a knowing: *"when he knows how"*. The verse marks the moment a person can tell evil from good and turn from the one to the other.; The verse ties the eating to that knowing: he eats *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"*. The oracle itself says what curds and honey are. *"In that day … because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey"* (v21–22). It is the food of those left in the land after the Lord has swept it with *"the king of Assyria"*: vineyards turned to *"briers and thorns"*, hills *"where cattle are let loose"* (v23–25). The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats with those who are left, and eats from abundance, in a land stripped of what it had.

19653.text: Isaiah 1:29 — "the oaks that you desired … the gardens that you have chosen": The oracle opens as a lawsuit: *"Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth"* (v2). The charge goes to the inner being: *"Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me"* (v2); *"The ox knows its owner … but Israel does not know, my people do not understand"* (v3); *"The whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint"* (v5); Their worship goes on, and the Lord refuses it: *"I do not delight in the blood of bulls"* (v11); *"your appointed feasts my soul hates"* (v14); *"even though you make many prayers, I will not listen"* (v15).; Then the choice is laid before them, in the same two-sided shape as Isa 7:15: *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"* (v16–17); *"Come now, let us reason together"*, with the offer that sins *"like scarlet"* shall be *"as white as snow"* (v18); the two outcomes: *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*; *"but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (v19–20); Being willing, and refusing (here H3985, a different word from Isa 7), are the two sides of the choice. Eating, and being eaten, are its two outcomes.; The oracle ends with those who did not take the offer. v29–31 is figurative speech, and the figure is the point: *"they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen"*; *"you shall be like an oak whose leaf withers, and like a garden without water"*; *"the strong shall become tinder, and his work a spark, and both of them shall burn together"*; The things they desired and chose become the picture of what they themselves become. They chose oaks and gardens, and they become a withering oak and a garden with no water. The choice comes back as an image of the chooser. The last line goes further: the strong man’s own *"work"* is the spark that sets him alight. What he made burns him, *"with none to quench them"*.; Shame comes first in the verse: *"ashamed"*, *"blush"* (H0954, H2659). The chooser is ashamed of the very thing that was desired and chosen. What drew the desire becomes the cause of the shame.

19683.text: Acts 15:22, 25 — "it seemed good … having come to one accord, to choose men": The choosing ends a dispute that went to the heart of the faith. Some taught *"Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved"* (v1), and there was *"no small dissension and debate"* (v2).; At the council the first word about choosing is God's. Peter says *"Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (v7). It is the same verb as the church's later choosing (G1586). He goes on: *"God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit … having cleansed their hearts by faith"* (v8–9). The assembly *"fell silent"* and *"listened"* (v12). James gives his judgement from the prophets (v13–21).; Then the church chooses: *"it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch"* (v22). The letter says how they came to it: *"it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you"* (v25). "One accord" (G3661) is a single shared mind. The same verb for "seemed good" (G1380) then joins them to the Spirit: *"it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"* (v28).; So the church's choosing: follows God's choosing, in the same verb; follows listening in silence; comes from one accord; is joined to what seemed good to the Holy Spirit; The outcome is in the hearers' hearts: *"when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement"* (v31). Judas and Silas *"encouraged and strengthened the brothers"* (v32), and were *"sent off in peace"* (v33). The letter answers the *"unsettling"* of their *"minds"* (v24).

19953.text: Knowing a choice, and arguing from it. In the dispute at Jerusalem Peter appeals to what the assembly knows: *"you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (Act 15:7). The purpose of God's choosing one man lies in others: that they hear and believe. Their hearts were known by God and *"cleansed … by faith"* (15:8–9). The debate ends in silence and listening (15:12), and the assembly's own choosing follows (15:25).

20010.text: The forms: plotting (*"as they scheme together against me, as they plot to take my life"*, Psa 31:13); imagining (*"they imagine the worst for me"*, Psa 41:7); using the tongue (*"Your tongue plots destruction"*, Psa 52:2; *"let us strike him with the tongue"*, Jer 18:18); group plans (*"Come, let us cut her off from being a nation!"*, Jer 48:2; *"they made plans to put him to death"*, Joh 11:53); against God himself (*"What do you plot against the Lord?"*, Nah 1:9)

20031.text: 10.10 Relating to others, new section *Plotting against another* | Planned in the heart (Psa 140:2; Zec 7:10; 8:17). Done together (Psa 31:13; Jer 48:2; Joh 11:53; 12:10–11; Eze 11:2; Dan 11:25, 27; Jer 49:30). Aimed at the quiet and the weak (Psa 10:2; 35:20; 37:12; Eze 38:10–11). Hidden behind something friendly (Neh 6:2–3; 1Sa 18:25). Accusing the other of a plan (Neh 6:6, 8–9). The one plotted against: not knowing (Jer 11:19–20); praying to be guarded (Psa 140:4, 8; 35:4); trusting (Psa 31:14–15); another pleading (Est 8:3; 9:24); another stopping it (Act 27:42–43). Named and checked (Pro 24:8–9; 30:32–33; Deu 19:19–20) | New section

20120.text: A resolve reached after weighing, then turned. *"her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly"* (Mat 1:19). The next verse: *"But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream"* (1:20). The resolve was still being weighed, and God redirected it.

20133.text: God's call: *"In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength." But you were unwilling* (Isa 30:15); *"Israel would not submit to me"* (Psa 81:11); *"not willing to listen to me: because all the house of Israel have a hard forehead and a stubborn heart"* (Eze 3:7).

20135.text: Isaiah 30 joins the refusing will to planning in one passage. It opens: *"Ah, stubborn children," declares the Lord, "who carry out a plan, but not mine"* (Isa 30:1). It goes on to the people *"unwilling to hear the instruction of the Lord"* (30:9) and ends the oracle with *"But you were unwilling"* (30:15). Here refusing God's word goes with carrying out a plan of one's own. This is the closest the Hebrew verses come to your continuum, and it is a single passage, not a pattern.

20160.text: Rest: *"This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose"; yet they would not hear* (Isa 28:12). *"In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength." But you were unwilling* (Isa 30:15).

20164.text: What the refusal goes with. In these passages the "no" to God is placed beside something the people chose or planned instead: *"But you were unwilling, and you said, 'No! We will flee upon horses'"* (Isa 30:15–16). The refusal is said in their own words, together with their own plan. The chapter opened with *"stubborn children … who carry out a plan, but not mine"* (30:1). They told the prophets, *"Do not prophesy to us what is right; speak to us smooth things"* (30:10).; *"Israel would not submit to me. So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels"* (Psa 81:11–12).; *"Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the Lord, would have none of my counsel and despised all my reproof, therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way, and have their fill of their own devices"* (Pro 1:29–31).; *"None of them cast away the detestable things their eyes feasted on"* (Eze 20:8).; *"a hard forehead and a stubborn heart"* (Eze 3:7).

20179.text: Joseph. *"being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream"* (Mat 1:19–20). He was unwilling to shame her, he resolved, and he went on considering. Then God spoke into the considering.

20207.text: 2.2 Passages where Scripture itself puts them together: Pro 1:29–31. Did not choose the fear of the Lord, would have none of my counsel, are filled with their own devices: choosing, willing and devising in one sentence. Earlier in the same chapter, *"if sinners entice you, do not consent. If they say, 'Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood'"* (1:10–11) puts the will's "no" right against a group plot. That is plotting as written in 10.10.; Psa 81:11–12. Would not submit, given over to stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels.; Isa 30:1, 9, 15–16. A plan *"but not mine"*; unwilling to hear; unwilling, and *"No! We will flee upon horses."* The refusal and the people's own plan are in their own mouth together.; 1Ch 28:19–21. The plan from the hand of the Lord, and *"every willing man who has skill"*. This is the positive pairing: a plan given, and the willing who carry it out.; Gen 24:5–8. Planning ahead allows for another person's will (*"Perhaps the woman may not be willing"*).; 2Sa 13:24–28. A planner presses another's will until it gives way, and the plan goes on to murder.; Mat 1:19–20. Unwilling, then resolved, while still considering, then redirected by God.; Act 12:3–5. Herod's intending is set beside the church's prayer.; 2Co 1:15–17. Wanting, then plans, then the question of a divided word.; Act 27:42–43. One man's wish against a group's plan.; Dan 4:27–35. Counsel offered and not taken; the human will made absolute; the Most High *"does according to his will"*; reason returned.

20218.text: *ʾāḇâ* | refusing God (Isa 30:15); refusing sin (Pro 1:10); refusing to harm the anointed (1Sa 26:23); refusing a gift for others' sake (2Sa 23:17); refusing a plea by force (2Sa 13:14); refusing in grief (2Sa 12:17); God not willing to destroy (2Ki 8:19); God not willing to forgive (Deu 29:20) | What is refused, and for whose sake. The passages give the reason each time: faith, fear, grief, honour, force, covenant, love, a stubborn heart

20240.text: Knowing and remembering.: The chosen are prayed for, that the eyes of their hearts be enlightened to know their hope (Eph 1:18).; Their knowledge of the truth accords with godliness (Tit 1:1).; Forgetting one's cleansing is blindness, and another works to keep them remembering (2Pe 1:9, 12–15).; Batch 1 had the chosen called to remember (Psa 105:5; Isa 44:21).

20370.text: Jeremiah 8:3: "Death shall be preferred to life": > Q1 citation: ⚠ Check. Ch 2 *Wanting to die*: "Under judgment, death is wished for and withheld". The verse says death "shall be preferred" (H0977, Niphal: *shall be chosen*). "Wished for" softens the choosing word, and "withheld" belongs to Rev 9:6 only, not to Jer 8:3.; >; > Q2 M64: Include: corroborates and adds. Corroborates Ch 2 *Wanting to die*. New: the preference is a choosing word, and the Lord declares it as part of a judgment, after the people had loved, served and gone after other things (v2).; >; > Q3 other M-codes: M25 life/death: carried in Ch 2. M58 evil, M43 declares, M72 hosts: no.; This follows the Topheth judgment (7:30–34). The bones of kings, priests, prophets and people are brought out and spread *"before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they have loved and served, which they have gone after, and which they have sought and worshiped"* (8:2).; Then: *"Death shall be preferred to life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family in all the places where I have driven them"* (8:3).; "Preferred" is H0977 in the Niphal: death *shall be chosen* (literal sense of the Niphal) rather than life. The remnant prefer death, and the Lord declares it as part of the judgment.

20381.text: 2 Samuel 14:14: "he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast": > Q1 citation: ❗ Needs attention. The words are Joab's: "Joab put the words in her mouth" (14:3), for a pretended plea ("Pretend to be a mourner", 14:2). Ch 2 ("A wise woman put it to David in a picture") does not say so. 10.4 presents the line as a plain statement about God, and adds "those who have put themselves outside", which is not in the verse ("the banished one"; in v13 it is the king who has not brought him home). Both places need restating.; >; > Q2 M64: Include: new. New: one passage holds three devisings: Joab's scheme to move the king, the king's decision ("planned", v13), and God's devising as the woman declares it (v14).; >; > Q3 other M-codes: M25 die: carried in Ch 2. M47 life and M06 "means" (H4284): no. In the passage, the pretence (v2): a pointer for 10.11 *Hiding and disclosing* and M14 when taken up.; The setting is a staged plea: Joab knew *"the king's heart went out to Absalom"* (v1).; He told the woman of Tekoa to *"Pretend to be a mourner"* (v2), and *"put the words in her mouth"* (v3).; Inside the story she tells, she asks: *"Why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God?"* (v13).; Then she says v14: *"We must all die … But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"*. "Devises" is H2803G.; David sees through it: *"Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?"* (v19). *"In order to change the course of things your servant Joab did this"* (v20).

20382.text: Reading: in this passage, devising goes on in three places: Joab's plan to move the king; the king's own decision, as the woman puts it (v13, "planned"); God's devising, which she declares (v14); I read v14 as a true saying put to work in a human scheme. The narrative's use of v14 is not wrong. The setting adds the human devising around it.

20490.text: 9.3 From thought to action (Claude's reading): The verses trace a path from thought to deed: Arising. Thoughts come, often in the night (Dan 2:29; Job 4:13; Ezek 38:10; Luke 24:38).; Lodging. They stay and are dwelt on (Jer 4:14).; Reckoning. They weigh up and value things (Isa 53:4; 1 Sam 1:13).; Devising. They take the form of a plan (Ezek 38:10b; Ps 36:4).; Expression. Tongue, lips and eyes: "your tongue plots" (Ps 52:2), "devise words of deceit" (Ps 35:20), "winks his eyes plans" (Prov 16:30), "whisper … imagine the worst" (Ps 41:7).; Action. Hand and feet: "when the morning dawns, they perform it" (Mic 2:1); "a heart that devises … feet that make haste" (Prov 6:18); "their feet run to evil … their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity" (Isa 59:7).; The same path also runs toward good: "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies" (Ps 119:59).

20534.text: Face: Devising against; Verses: Psa 36:4; 52:2; 41:7; 35:4, 20; 21:11; 140:2, 4; 10:2; Mic 2:1; Eze 11:2; 38:10; Nah 1:9, 11; Neh 6:2, 6; Jer 11:19; 18:18; 48:2; Est 8:3; 9:24–25; 1Sa 18:25; 2Sa 14:13; Dan 11:24–25; Hos 7:15; Pro 16:30; 24:8; Zec 7:10; 8:17; Gen 50:20a; What differs: Aimed against a named person or God, nearly every time. Joined with arrogance (Psa 10:2), whispering together (41:7), tongue and lips (52:2; Pro 16:30), the bed (Psa 36:4; Mic 2:1), envy of a rival (1Sa 18:25, after the anger of 18:8). Against the one who trained them: "Although I trained and strengthened their arms, yet they devise evil against me" (Hos 7:15); Why (basis): The "against" is stated (S). Ingratitude turns into a plot (S, Hos 7:15)
